f: The title-plan practice guide was updated on 13 July 2026.
The guide applies to England and Wales.
A registered estate's property register description refers to a plan based on Ordnance Survey mapping.
The title plan is one of three elements of a registered title.
A title plan must be viewed together with the register.
Using OS mapping helps relate individual title plans to one another.
Adjoining title plans may be based on different OS map editions.
HM Land Registry retains historic editions of title plans.
The title plan graphically supports the property description.
The title plan identifies the general extent of the registered land.
A title plan may identify easements, covenants or removed land referenced by the register.
The title plan was previously called the filed plan.
Title plans show general boundaries unless a boundary is determined under section 60.
Relating franchises and lordship titles do not have title plans.
A profit a prendre in gross title may in some circumstances lack a title plan.
Title plans fall mainly into vector, raster and drawer/canister categories.
All newly created title plans are vector plans.
Vector title plans are electronically stored and described as intelligent.
A raster title plan is an electronic image of a former paper plan.
Raster title plans are not intelligent.
Drawer/canister title plans exist in paper form only.
Drawer/canister plans generally belong to old registered titles.
A title plan is based on information in the original title deeds.
Each registered extent is allocated a unique title number.
Land is not routinely surveyed when deed plans and OS detail are compatible.
Undefined boundaries may be plotted with pecked lines.
Urban title plans are usually prepared at 1:1250.
Rural title plans are usually prepared at 1:2500.
Large rural title plans may use 1:5000.
Large rural title plans may use 1:10000.
An enlargement may be added where a small area needs clearer depiction.
Most historic paper title plans were prepared on B4 paper.
Plans larger than B4 could use pages or flaps.
Vector title plans can range from A4 to A0.
Registered land is normally shown by red edging.
Red edging normally follows the inside of the physical or plotted boundary line.
Exceptional extents may use outside edging or pink tinting.
Small wall sites may use exceptional depiction where normal edging is impractical.
An excluded island is shown by green tinting or hatching with red edging.
An excluded island is accompanied by an explanatory note.
Registrations containing only part of a building receive an explanatory register note.
Complex floor levels may use a supplementary larger-scale plan.
Land removed to another title is usually edged green.
The new title number can be shown in green.
Green tinting may be used without displaying the new title number.
Most lease plans lodged today are digitally produced at larger scale.
A tenant title plan may show only the building outline.
External lease areas such as parking may be shown separately.
Large developments may record lease extents on the landlord's plan.
A lease, register and title plan must be read together.
Title-plan dimensions are shown only when present in deed plans.
Displayed dimensions do not convert a general boundary into an exact boundary.
Dimension reference points may disappear or change.
Dimensions from deed plans are no longer routinely reproduced.
Historic imperial measurements have not been converted wholesale.
Requested imperial-to-metric conversions are made to four decimal places.
Title plans can include tinting, hatching, coloured edges, numbering and broken lines.
A clearly identifiable easement may be described verbally rather than with a plan reference.
Existing deed colour references are reproduced where practicable.
Specific drainage rights are normally shown by a coloured broken line.
Developing-estate easements may be covered by a general verbal register entry.
Intricate easements or covenants may require an enlargement or supplementary plan.
OS field or parcel numbers have no title significance unless used as plan references.
A relevant OS number can be circled in blue with a matching register entry.
Brace symbols link areas forming part of the same reference.
HM Land Registry receives Ordnance Survey map updates daily.
Title plans are not routinely updated when OS mapping changes.
A title plan remains in its original form until title activity justifies updating.
Boundary amendments generally require proprietor agreement or a specific application.
A replacement plan can be prepared with an explanatory register note.
Later OS mapping may be used when land has been sold from a title.
Only a small percentage of applications or enquiries require surveys.
HM Land Registry surveys are carried out by Ordnance Survey.
A survey may supply new topographic detail.
A survey may check mapping accuracy where deeds conflict with existing detail.
A survey may record measurements, boundary age/nature, land use, occupation and photographs.
Affected parties are notified when a survey is required.
OS requires access and hazard information through its online form.
The surveyor checks OS mapping and updates it where needed.
The surveyor does not have detailed knowledge of the registration application.
Information supplied by attendees is not recorded by the surveyor.
A determined-boundary plan must clearly show the boundary extent by suitable colouring or edging.
The plan must identify start, end and turning points.
The plan must include a statement describing the determined line.
The plan must show enough surrounding detail for OS-map location.
The plan must show orientation, for example a north point.
The determined-boundary plan must state its scale.
The preferred scale is no smaller than 1:200.
The plan should ideally be no larger than A3.
The plan must not contain an accuracy disclaimer.
Measurement-based plans require plus or minus 10 mm accuracy.
Measurements must be horizontal, not measured along a slope.
At least two defined permanent reference points are required.
Permanent features should reasonably remain for at least ten years.
Only National Grid coordinates are accepted for coordinate-based plans.
National Grid coordinates require plus or minus 300 mm absolute accuracy.
National Grid coordinates require plus or minus 10 mm relative accuracy.
Coordinate pairs record eastings before northings.
Coordinate plans require certification by OS or a suitably qualified professional.
Article 4 data may be supplied as CSV.
Article 4 data may be supplied as GeoJSON.
Article 4 data may be supplied as GML.
Article 4 data may be supplied as GeoPackage.
Article 4 data may be served through OGC WFS or an ArcGIS API.
Uppercase field-name characters are converted to lowercase.
The direction dataset needs at least one row per direction.
Direction references must be unique within a provider dataset.
Direction references must remain stable during updates.
document-url must identify the authoritative order or notice.
The documentation page must include a short description.
Each direction must have a unique documentation URL.
Anchor fragments may provide unique URLs on a shared page.
end-date stays blank while a direction remains active.
entry-date records the last entity update.
For never-updated entities, entry-date equals start-date.
The area dataset needs at least one row per area.
Area geometry is a polygon or multipolygon.
Data must be published on the official planning authority website.
Published data must use a clear and understandable format.
The webpage must state Open Government Licence terms.
An endpoint may be a hosted file.
An endpoint may be a live API feed.
An ArcGIS URL includes a numeric layer identifier.
Publishers should update data without changing the endpoint URL.
The webpage must link the endpoint, summarise coverage and state the licence.
Legal-document records require a document-url pointing directly to the file.
The DTM dataset states no public access constraints.
The DTM dataset is licensed under the Open Government Licence.
The dataset carries Environment Agency copyright/database attribution.
The dataset update frequency is annual.
LIDAR is described as an airborne mapping technique.
Detailed terrain models span resolutions from 25 cm to 2 m.
The LIDAR dataset vertical accuracy is plus or minus 15 cm RMSE.
The dataset coordinate reference system is EPSG:27700.
The published latitude extent begins at 49.943.
The published latitude extent ends at 55.816.
The published longitude extent begins at -6.236.
The published longitude extent ends at 2.072.
A DTM 1m WMS service is listed.
A metadata survey-index WMS is listed.
A metadata survey-index WFS is listed.
A DTM 1m WCS service is listed.
A DTM 1m WMTS service is listed.
An OGC API Features service is listed.
The dataset period runs from 6 June 2000 to 2 April 2022.
Related datasets include 2 m and 10 m DTM products.
A related 1 m DSM dataset is listed.
WCS serves and retrieves multidimensional coverages.
WCS is intended for clients including QGIS and ArcGIS Desktop.
WCS can return raw elevation pixel data.
WCS and WMS provide an open, non-proprietary alternative to Esri image services.
ArcGIS users may need to enter raster statistics manually.
Published DTM1 statistics are min -409.05, max 978.05, mean 104.63 and standard deviation 107.52.
OS Terrain 50 is an Open Data product.
The product is designed for landscape visualisation and large-area analysis.
The product is published as grid and contour data.
Grid and contour outputs use the same source data.
Both outputs use 10 km by 10 km tiles.
Tile names quote the south-west National Grid reference.
Grid data uses regular 50 m post spacing.
Contour data uses 10 m standard contour intervals.
Contour data includes mean high-water and mean low-water boundaries.
Grid data is available as ASCII Grid.
Grid data is available as GML 3.2.1 simple-features level 0.
Contours are available as GML 3.2.1 simple-features level 0.
Contours are available as Esri Shapefile.
Contours are available as MBTiles vector tiles.
Contour vector tiles are supplied nationally in one MBTiles file.
The vector-tile set is designed for efficient, fast rendering.
Vector tiles provide a seamless zooming experience.
Vector tiles use Web Mercator EPSG:3857.
The schema includes contour_line, spot_height and land_water_boundary layers.
Each vector-tile layer includes an id attribute.
Each vector-tile layer includes a property_value attribute.
The documented attributes are mapped at zoom levels 9 through 14, not 0 through 8.
